newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rocky road seen ahead for Japan long-term banks.
newsitem.headline: Rocky road seen ahead for Japan long-term banks.

text.p: Japan's long-term credit banks may lose the competitive advantage they enjoy from issuing bank debentures when "Big Bang" financial reforms are implemented, analysts say.

The three long-term credit banks should therefore decrease their reliance on the traditional business of offering long-term, fixed-rate loans to big corporations based on long-term prime rates, they said.

The long-term prime rate is charged on loans of one year and longer to the banks' most creditworthy customers. Bank debentures are a key tool used by the long-term credit banks to raise funds for lending to customers, and the gap between what the banks pay out on debentures and receive in interest payments on their loans is crucial to profitability.

The Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ), the largest of the three long-term credit banks, said on Monday that it would set its long-term prime lending rate for May at 3.1 percent, compared with 2.5 percent for April, from Wednesday.

The other two long-term credit banks -- Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd and Nippon Credit Bank Ltd -- said on Tuesday they would also raise their long-term prime lending rates for May by 0.6 percentage point to 3.1 percent.

"It is true that big companies are raising more funds in the capital market. Long-term credit banks would need to offset decreases in revenue by strengthening other areas, such as the securities business," said Yoshinobu Yamada, a senior analyst at Merrill Lynch in Tokyo.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) does not allow ordinary banks to issue bank debentures, with the exception of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd (BOTM). But a MOF advisory panel is considering lifting this ban as part of Japan's proposed "Big Bang" financial reforms.
If banks with credit ratings higher than long-term credit banks were allowed to issue bank debentures, that may bite into long-term credit banks' profit margins, analysts said.
For more than 20 years, the IBJ has been setting its long-term prime rate 0.9 of a percentage point above the coupon rate for its new five-year bank debentures.

However, market forces had already forced the LTCB and NCB to abandon their practice of setting the debenture coupon rate in line with the IBJ. Currently, the LTCB sets its long-term prime rate 0.6 percentage point above its debenture coupon. As for NCB, the spread between its long-term prime rate and the debenture coupon is only 0.15 percentage point.

Meanwhile, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said on Tuesday it had set the coupon rate for its May five-year debenture at 2.1 percent, 0.1 of a percentage point lower that of the IBJ debenture. This was the first time a bank has set a coupon rate for a debenture at a level lower than that of IBJ's debenture.
Analysts said long-term credit banks are also suffering as a result of a preference by big firms for direct finance.

"About half of the loans by long-term credit banks are for big corporations. An increasing number of big firms, however, are choosing to raise long-term funds directly from the capital market by issuing straight bonds," said Nozomu Kunishige, a senior analyst at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo.
Big firms with good debt ratings can raise long-term funds more cheaply by issuing bonds than by borrowing from long-term credit banks at the long-term prime rate, analysts said.
The long-term prime rate had stood at a record low of 2.5 percent from December 1996 to April, but some blue-chip firms have launched five-year straight bonds with coupon rates below 2.5 percent.
For example, Skylark, a restaurant chain operator, recently launched 10 billion yen worth of five-year straight bonds at a coupon rate of 2.45 percent.

But Merrill Lynch's Yamada said financial liberalisation could also have benefits for the long-term credit banks. "Big Bang is not all negative for long-term credit banks. It would allow them to do more securities business," he said.
